sections.learningObjectives:
- Describe controlled substance scheduling concepts.
- Explain secure storage and access control for medications.
- Recognize diversion-prevention and inventory-logging practices.
- Apply safety-first escalation and policy-following when discrepancies or suspected diversion arise.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Think of a controlled substance like the keys to a car. Most medicines are like groceries you can just buy, but a controlled substance is kept under lock and key because it is powerful and could be misused.

### Question 2

Imagine sorting toys into boxes by how careful you have to be with them. The most delicate or dangerous toys get the most careful boxes, and the safest ones can go on an open shelf.

### Question 3

Think of five drawers, labeled I through V. Drawer I holds the most tightly controlled items, and by the time you reach drawer V, the rules are gentler.

### Question 4

Schedule I is like the very top shelf in a locked cabinet: the strongest, most dangerous items with no everyday use go there and almost nobody gets to touch them.

### Question 5

Picture a staircase. At the bottom step (Schedule II) you have very strong medicine that needs tight control. As you walk up the steps, each medicine is a little gentler and used more freely in everyday care.

### Question 6

It is like a very important document: the more valuable and dangerous it is, the more you lock it up and count it, instead of leaving it on your desk.

### Question 7

Think of a tool that has no job in the workshop. Because it has no accepted job, it stays locked away, while tools with real jobs are allowed out under supervision.

### Question 8

There is a special 'medicine police' at the national level whose job is to watch over powerful medicines and make sure only the right people handle them.

### Question 9

Only the person with the special license can write the special ticket for a controlled medicine, just like only a licensed driver can drive a big truck.

### Question 10

Your job is like a careful mail carrier: you deliver and record the letter, but you never rewrite what is inside it.

### Question 11

Think of a school rule that everyone must wear shoes, and your house adds a rule to also wear socks. You follow both, and the stricter one wins.

### Question 12

You lock up things that are dangerous or easy to misuse, like a parent locking up cleaning supplies, not because they are fancy but because they can hurt someone if mishandled.

### Question 13

Diversion is like someone taking food from a food bank that was meant for families in need and using it themselves instead. The medicine was meant for patients, and someone is taking it for the wrong reason.

### Question 14

Think of a strict movie ticket: you need a fresh ticket for each show. You cannot just keep reusing one old ticket over and over.

### Question 15

All squares are rectangles, but not all rectangles are squares. All controlled substances need special prescribing, but not all prescription medicines are controlled.

### Question 16

You might keep a candy bowl out for everyone, but you keep your family's important papers in a safe inside a locked closet—two locks for the things that matter most.

### Question 17

You keep your most valuable things in a locked box, not sitting out on the front porch where anyone could grab them.

### Question 18

A locked door keeps out people who should not go in, while people with a key can still come and go safely.

### Question 19

When a valuable package arrives, you sign for it, write it down, and lock it up right away instead of leaving it on the doorstep.

### Question 20

Only the grown-ups who need to get in have a key; you do not make copies for everyone in the house.

### Question 21

It is like keeping ice cream safe: it needs the freezer to stay cold AND a lock so no one takes it without permission.

### Question 22

You lock the front door every time you leave, even if you are only walking to the mailbox for one minute.

### Question 23

Not every family member gets a key to the safe—only the ones who truly need it.

### Question 24

You keep the important documents in their own labeled folder, not jumbled with old coupons, so you can always find and count them fast.

### Question 25

You can leave the box of bandages on the shelf, but you lock up the strong medicine—because one is easy to misuse and the other is not.

### Question 26

You would not leave a precious ring in a classroom cubby where any student could reach it; you would keep it locked away.

### Question 27

A present from a visitor still has to follow the same house rules—if it is a controlled medicine, it goes in the locked cabinet and gets written down.

### Question 28

You would not throw old medicine in the kitchen trash where a child or pet could find it; there is a special, safe way to get rid of it.

### Question 29

Like a first-aid kit that must stay sealed so you can tell if anyone has used it, the emergency medicine kit stays closed and gets counted on a schedule.

### Question 30

When you receive a package, signing for it is like taking a picture of the handoff so everyone knows exactly who had it and when.

### Question 31

You lock your piggy bank in a drawer AND lock the house door AND turn on the alarm—layers of locks working together.

### Question 32

You keep the salt and sugar in clearly marked jars so you never mix them up when baking.

### Question 33

It is like a checkbook where you write down every deposit and every purchase, so you always know exactly how much money is left.

### Question 34

It is like writing down who borrowed each library book, so you can tell if a book goes missing and who had it last.

### Question 35

Two people count the money in a store's cash register together so no one can make a mistake—or take some—without the other noticing.

### Question 36

You write down what you spent the moment you spend it, not at the end of the year when you have forgotten.

### Question 37

A good note says who, what, when, and how much—like a detective's notebook that can solve the mystery if something goes missing.

### Question 38

It is like checking that the money in the jar matches the total written in your notebook; if they do not match, you stop and figure out why.

### Question 39

If one cookie is missing from the jar and the list says the jar should be full, you tell a grown-up right away instead of pretending the list was wrong.

### Question 40

It is like a scoreboard that updates every time someone scores, so you always know the current score.

### Question 41

You keep your important homework in a folder in your backpack, not scattered on the sidewalk where it could blow away.

### Question 42

You would not put your name on homework someone else did and say it was yours—your signature means you saw it and it is true.

### Question 43

At a school bake sale, one person counts the money, another writes it down, and a third locks it up—so no one person controls everything.

### Question 44

You would not leave blank pages in your diary for someone else to write on later; you keep the record complete and safe.

### Question 45

When you make a mistake in your notebook, you draw one neat line through it and write the fix next to it, instead of scribbling it into a black blob.

### Question 46

A blank checkbook is locked away because someone could write a fake check; a blank prescription pad is the same idea for medicine.

### Question 47

Each person has their own locker combination, so the school always knows who opened which locker and when.

### Question 48

If you drop and break a cookie, you tell someone and write it down instead of pretending you ate it.

### Question 49

The inventory is the cookies actually in the jar, and the log is your list of how many should be there—they should always agree.

### Question 50

Diversion is like taking a library book that was meant for everyone and keeping it for yourself—the medicine was meant for patients, and someone is taking it for the wrong reason.

### Question 51

If someone keeps taking cookies meant for the whole class, soon there are no cookies left, everyone is upset, and nobody trusts the cookie jar.

### Question 52

If cookies keep disappearing from the jar and no one admits taking them, that is a clue something is wrong.

### Question 53

If a friend keeps asking for extra dessert before dinner, you would check with the grown-up in charge instead of sneaking them more.

### Question 54

If you think someone is doing something wrong, you tell a trusted teacher or adult instead of handling it all by yourself.

### Question 55

You cannot 'borrow' a cookie from the class jar and put a different one back later—taking it for yourself is still taking it.

### Question 56

If the cookie list always has smudged or missing names, you would wonder if someone is not writing things down on purpose.

### Question 57

You take a message for the grown-up in charge rather than making a big decision you are not allowed to make.

### Question 58

If a permission slip from a parent looks scribbled on, the teacher checks with the parent instead of just accepting it.

### Question 59

A blank check is locked up because someone could write a fake amount; a blank prescription pad is locked up for the same reason.

### Question 60

If a cookie falls on the floor, you show someone and throw it away together, so everyone knows it was really dropped and not secretly eaten.

### Question 61

The assistant is like the scorekeeper who carefully records the game but does not make the rules or play for the team.

### Question 62

Only a person with the right license can write the special medicine ticket, just like only a referee can blow the whistle.

### Question 63

Borrowing without asking is still taking, even if you promise to put it back next week.

### Question 64

If a note from a teacher looks unusual, the office checks with the teacher before acting on it.

### Question 65

A classroom suggestion box lets students speak up without fear, so problems get fixed before they grow.

### Question 66

A cookie that is not on the list can vanish and no one will ever know it was there.

### Question 67

A relay race can be lost at any handoff, so every runner must be careful—the same is true at every step of a medicine's journey.

### Question 68

Access control is like a members-only club door: only people with the right card can get in.

### Question 69

If only a few people have the key, then when something goes missing you know who to ask.

### Question 70

You keep a list of who has a house key, and if someone moves out, you change the locks.

### Question 71

Everyone has their own locker combination, so the school knows whose locker was opened and when.

### Question 72

You would not leave your bike unlocked 'just for a minute' outside a store.

### Question 73

When a club member quits, their membership card is turned in so they cannot get back in.

### Question 74

A tablet locks itself when you stop using it, so a stranger cannot pick it up and pretend to be you.

### Question 75

A moat around the castle plus a lock on the treasure room—both help keep the treasure safe.

### Question 76

You get a key only for the rooms you need to use, not a master key to every room in the building.

### Question 77

Guests in your house stay with you; they do not wander into the room where valuables are kept.

### Question 78

You keep the candy jar in the kitchen where only family goes, not on the front porch where anyone walking by could reach in.

### Question 79

It is like a security camera for computer actions—it shows who did what and when.

### Question 80

You check the locks and make sure the spare keys are all accounted for on a regular schedule, not just after a break-in.

### Question 81

If you find the front door open in the morning, you check inside and tell a grown-up instead of just closing it and walking away.

### Question 82

Even in a family, each person has their own phone password so everyone knows who did what on which device.

### Question 83

Your locker combination stays secret and you change it sometimes, so no one can guess it or see it written down.

### Question 84

You only open the drawers in the kitchen that you need for cooking, not every drawer in the house.

### Question 85

You would not post a map of where the treasure is hidden on the front door.

### Question 86

If the scoreboard breaks, the referee keeps score with pencil and paper so the game is still fair.

### Question 87

A family fire drill means everyone knows what to do before there is smoke, not in the middle of it.

### Question 88

You write important notes in pen, not pencil, so no one can sneakily change what was written.

### Question 89

You can pass a note to the teacher about what your friend wants, but only the teacher decides whether to allow it.

### Question 90

You count the expensive jewelry in the safe every single day, but you only glance at the paper clips once a month.
